name: glam (SIMD 3D math types)
baseline: nalgebra 0.35.0 small fixed-size f32 vectors, matrices and transforms
verdict_reason: glam is 2x to 12x faster than nalgebra on 4x4 matrix multiply, inverse and determinant, affine inverse and ray-sphere tests, but in the same run it is 4.1x slower on vector3 length and 2.2x slower on vector3 normalize. The win is real for matrix and transform work, not across the board.
tier_reason: mathbench is public, and the README states the rustc version, RUSTFLAGS, CPU and every library version; it is written by glam's author.
claimed_speedup: ns per op, glam vs nalgebra: matrix4 mul matrix4 3.2445 vs 6.3150, matrix4 inverse 10.9287 vs 26.7860, matrix4 determinant 3.4266 vs 40.7346, transform3 inverse 5.8707 vs 26.5732, ray-sphere intersection 8.0682 vs 17.5249 (1.95x, 2.45x, 11.9x, 4.53x, 2.17x) (derived from page data). Slower: vector3 length 1.2799 vs 0.3107, vector3 normalize 2.1077 vs 0.9517 ns
workload: mathbench scalar benchmarks on f32: one operation applied over batches of 16 or 1,024 inputs (10,000 for ray-sphere and Euler), criterion timings per operation.
toolchain: rustc 1.99.0 (b940084d7 2026-09-28), default bench profile plus RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native'
platforms: SIMD storage on x86, x86_64, aarch64 and wasm32/wasm64 (SSE2 by default on x86_64, NEON on aarch64, simd128 opt-in); scalar elsewhere
one_liner: 3D math library with SIMD-backed Vec4/Mat4/Quat; 2-12x faster than nalgebra on matrix and transform ops, slower on some vector ops.
how_it_is_fast: Vec3A, Vec4, Mat4 and Quat are stored in 16-byte SIMD registers and implemented with SSE2 or NEON intrinsics, so a 4x4 multiply or inverse runs as a handful of vector instructions. nalgebra's generic code relies on the auto-vectorizer for fixed-size types, which handles matrix-matrix work less well.
use_it_when: Games, graphics and simulation code built on 2D-4D f32 or f64 vectors, matrices, quaternions and affine transforms.
Hot loops over 4x4 matrix multiply, inverse or transform inverse.
skip_it_when: You need general N-dimensional or dynamically sized linear algebra; glam stops at 4x4.
Your hot path is vector3 length or normalize, where nalgebra measured faster in this run.
caveats: All published numbers use target-cpu=native on a Ryzen 7 3800X; default x86_64 builds get only SSE2.
mathbench is written by glam's author.
Microbenchmarks of single operations over small batches; whole-program gains depend on the mix of operations.
tradeoffs: Fixed set of types up to 4x4; no generic dimensions or scalar types beyond f32, f64 and integer vectors.
Vec3A and Mat3A are 16-byte aligned and padded, so they use more memory than packed [f32; 3].

evidence.quote: compiled with the `1.99.0 (b940084d7 2026-09-28)` Rust compiler with
RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' cargo bench --features scalar scalar
These benchmarks were performed on an [AMD Ryzen 7 3800X] CPU on Linux.
